ctw.text: Scientists have long suspected that sleep plays an important role in learning. During de{ep} sleep, t{he} brain rep{lays} information th{at} was gath{ered} during t{he} day a{nd} moves i{t} from temp{orary} to perm{anent} storage. In one experiment, students who slept after studying remembered more words than students who stayed awake. Researchers believe that certain brain waves help strengthen the connections between neurons. This may explain why students who sleep poorly often struggle in exams.

Public libraries offer much more than books. Many o{f} them le{nd} laptops, cam{eras}, and ev{en} musical instr{uments} to th{eir} members. So{me} libraries al{so} run fr{ee} classes o{n} topics such as cooking, coding, and personal finance. Because these services cost nothing, they are especially helpful for families with small budgets. In many towns, the library has become a meeting place where people of all ages can study, work, or simply relax.

Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This pheno{menon}, known a{s} the ur{ban} heat isl{and} effect, ari{ses} because asp{halt} and conc{rete} absorb so{lar} radiation dur{ing} the d{ay} and release it slowly at night. The scarcity of vegetation intensifies the problem, since plants cool their surroundings through evaporation. Municipal planners increasingly counteract the effect by installing reflective roofing materials and expanding green spaces, measures that can substantially reduce energy consumption during summer heat waves.

Honeybees have a remarkable way of sharing information. When a wor{ker} bee disc{overs} a go{od} source o{f} food, i{t} returns t{o} the hi{ve} and perf{orms} a spe{cial} dance. T{he} direction of the dance shows other bees which way to fly, while its length indicates how far away the flowers are. Scientists first described this behavior many decades ago, and later studies confirmed that bees can follow these instructions with surprising accuracy.

More people are riding bicycles to work than ever before. In ma{ny} cities, n{ew} bike la{nes} make t{he} trip sa{fer} and fas{ter}. Cycling i{s} cheap, a{nd} it al{so} helps peo{ple} stay fit without going to a gym. Some companies even pay workers a small bonus for leaving their cars at home. However, bad weather and long distances still keep many commuters from making the switch.

The placebo effect remains one of the most intriguing phenomena in medicine. Patients w{ho} receive a{n} inactive subs{tance} sometimes rep{ort} genuine improv{ements} in th{eir} symptoms, partic{ularly} when t{he} condition invo{lves} pain o{r} anxiety. Researchers attribute this response to expectation, which appears to trigger the release of natural chemicals in the brain. Consequently, clinical trials must compare new drugs against placebos rather than against no treatment at all, ensuring that observed benefits exceed those produced by belief alone.

Many animals use camouflage to avoid predators. Some ins{ects} look alm{ost} exactly li{ke} leaves o{r} twigs, wh{ich} makes th{em} very diff{icult} to s{ee}. Other ani{mals} can cha{nge} their colors to match their surroundings, as octopuses and some lizards do. Camouflage is not only useful for prey, however. Predators such as tigers use their striped coats to hide in tall grass while they wait for the right moment to attack.

Drinking enough water is important for good health. Our bod{ies} use wa{ter} to con{trol} temperature a{nd} to ca{rry} nutrients t{o} our ce{lls}. Many peo{ple} only dr{ink} when th{ey} feel thirsty, but by then the body may already need more water. Doctors suggest keeping a bottle nearby during the day. Fruits and vegetables also contain a lot of water, so they can help too.

Language extinction has accelerated dramatically over the past century. Linguists esti{mate} that rou{ghly} half o{f} the wor{ld's} languages co{uld} disappear wit{hin} the ne{xt} hundred ye{ars}. When a lang{uage} vanishes, commu{nities} frequently lose irreplaceable knowledge about local ecosystems, medicinal plants, and cultural traditions. Revitalization programs, which typically combine immersive schooling with digital archives, have achieved notable success in several regions, demonstrating that the decline is not necessarily irreversible when communities receive sustained institutional support.

academic.title: Mangrove Forests
academic.text:
Mangroves are trees that grow in the salty, shallow waters along tropical coastlines. Few plants can survive in such conditions, but mangroves have developed several unusual adaptations. Some species filter salt out of seawater through their roots, while others store excess salt in older leaves that eventually fall off. Because the muddy soil contains very little oxygen, many mangroves also grow special roots that stick up out of the mud like pencils, allowing the trees to absorb air directly.
These forests provide important benefits to both wildlife and people. Their dense root systems act as nurseries for young fish, which hide from predators among the roots until they are large enough to survive in open water. Mangroves also protect coastal communities: during storms, the tangled roots reduce the force of waves and help prevent the erosion of shorelines.
Despite these benefits, mangrove forests have declined significantly in recent decades. Large areas have been cleared to make room for shrimp farms and coastal development. Scientists warn that losing mangroves not only harms fish populations but also leaves coastal towns more vulnerable to storm damage.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why do some mangroves have roots that stick up out of the mud?
options: To take in oxygen from the air
To hold the trees in place during storms
questions.why: Der Schlamm enthält kaum Sauerstoff; die Wurzeln „absorb air directly“.

questions.q: The word "dense" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: dense = dicht.

options: To describe a threat to mangrove forests
To compare mangroves with coral reefs
To show one way mangroves benefit wildlife
To explain how mangroves obtain nutrients
questions.why: Junge Fische nutzen die Wurzeln als „nurseries“ – Beispiel für Nutzen für Tiere.

academic.title: Why Do We Yawn?
academic.text:
Everyone yawns, but scientists are still not sure why. For many years, people believed that yawning brings more oxygen into the body when we are tired. However, experiments have shown that breathing extra oxygen does not make people yawn less, so this explanation is probably wrong.
A newer idea is that yawning helps cool the brain. When we yawn, we take in a large amount of air, and the jaw stretches widely. This movement increases blood flow to the head and may lower the temperature of the brain slightly. In one study, people yawned less often when they held a cold pack against their forehead.
Yawning is also contagious. Seeing, hearing, or even reading about someone yawning can make us yawn too. Interestingly, people are more likely to "catch" a yawn from a family member or a close friend than from a stranger. Some researchers think this shows that contagious yawning is connected to empathy, the ability to understand how others feel.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The connection between sleep and body temperature
Different explanations for why people yawn
Why tired people need more oxygen
questions.why: Der Text stellt mehrere Erklärungen für das Gähnen vor.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why is the oxygen explanation probably wrong?
options: Yawning lowers the amount of oxygen in the body.
Breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning.
questions.why: „breathing extra oxygen does not make people yawn less“.

questions.q: The word "contagious" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: contagious = ansteckend.

questions.q: What did people do in the study mentioned in paragraph 2?
options: They held something cold against their forehead.
They watched videos of family members yawning.
questions.why: „held a cold pack against their forehead“.

questions.q: What can be inferred about contagious yawning?
options: It happens more often between people who are close.
It is a sign that a person is tired.
It only happens when people see someone yawn.
questions.why: Man „fängt“ das Gähnen eher bei Familie und Freunden.

academic.title: The Paradox of Choice
academic.text:
Conventional economic thinking holds that having more options is always beneficial: if an option is added that no one wants, people can simply ignore it. Yet a growing body of psychological research suggests that an abundance of options can, under certain conditions, undermine both decision-making and satisfaction.
In a widely cited field experiment, shoppers encountered a tasting booth offering either six or twenty-four varieties of jam. Although the larger display attracted more visitors, those who saw the smaller selection were roughly ten times more likely to make a purchase. The researchers proposed that comparing many similar alternatives imposes a cognitive burden that can lead people to postpone or avoid decisions altogether.
Even when people do choose, an extensive range of options may diminish their contentment. With more alternatives available, it becomes easier to imagine that a different selection would have been superior, and this anticipated regret can reduce the pleasure derived from the chosen item.
Subsequent studies, however, have complicated the picture. Several attempts to replicate the original findings produced weak or inconsistent effects, and analyses suggest that choice overload emerges mainly when options are difficult to compare or when decision-makers lack clear preferences. Experts in a particular domain, for instance, appear largely immune to it.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what does conventional economic thinking assume?
options: Additional options never make people worse off.
Unwanted options should be removed from stores.
questions.why: „having more options is always beneficial“ – man kann Unerwünschtes ignorieren.

questions.q: What was surprising about the result of the jam experiment?
options: Shoppers preferred jams with fewer ingredients.
Fewer people visited the smaller display.
Visitors spent more time tasting jam at the smaller display than at the larger one.
The larger display led to fewer purchases even though it attracted more visitors.
questions.why: Mehr Besucher, aber zehnmal weniger Käufe bei 24 Sorten.

questions.q: The word "diminish" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: diminish = verringern.

questions.q: Why does the author mention experts in the final paragraph?
options: To suggest that shoppers should consult experts before buying products
To show that choice overload does not affect everyone equally
To explain why the jam study was repeated
To argue that experts make worse decisions
questions.why: Experten sind „largely immune“ – der Effekt hängt von Bedingungen ab.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the author's view of the original findings?
options: They apply to all decisions people make.
They may hold only under certain conditions.
questions.why: Wiederholungen zeigten schwache Effekte; der Effekt tritt „mainly when …“ auf.

academic.title: Life at Hydrothermal Vents
academic.text:
In 1977, researchers exploring the floor of the Pacific Ocean made a discovery that overturned long-standing assumptions about life on Earth. Near volcanic openings called hydrothermal vents, where water heated by magma bursts from the seafloor at temperatures exceeding 350°C, they found thriving communities of giant tube worms, clams, and crabs.
The finding was puzzling because sunlight never penetrates these depths, and nearly all known ecosystems ultimately depend on photosynthesis. The explanation turned out to lie in chemosynthesis. Bacteria living around the vents derive energy from chemical reactions involving hydrogen sulfide, a compound abundant in the vent fluid but toxic to most organisms. These bacteria form the base of the food web; giant tube worms, which lack both a mouth and a digestive system, host billions of them inside their bodies and absorb the nutrients they produce.
The implications extend beyond marine biology. Because vent ecosystems function independently of the sun, some scientists have proposed that life on Earth may have originated in similar environments. The discovery has also encouraged the search for life on moons such as Europa and Enceladus, whose ice-covered oceans may conceal comparable hydrothermal activity.

questions.q: Why was the 1977 discovery surprising?
options: The water near the vents was colder than expected.
Clams had never been observed before.
The vents were located in the Pacific Ocean.
The animals survived without depending on sunlight.
questions.why: Fast alle Ökosysteme hängen an Photosynthese – hier gibt es kein Licht.

questions.q: The word "abundant" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: abundant = reichlich vorhanden.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how do giant tube worms obtain food?
options: From bacteria living inside their bodies
By eating smaller animals near the vents
By filtering plankton from the water
questions.why: Sie beherbergen Bakterien und nehmen deren Nährstoffe auf.

questions.q: What does the author indicate about hydrogen sulfide?
options: It is produced by the tube worms.
It is found mainly on Europa.
It is harmful to most living things.
questions.why: „toxic to most organisms“.

questions.q: Why does the author mention Europa and Enceladus?
options: To explain where vents were first discovered
To argue that life definitely exists there
To compare the temperatures of their oceans with those of Earth's oceans
To show that the discovery influenced the search for life elsewhere
questions.why: Die Entdeckung „encouraged the search for life on moons such as …“.

academic.title: The Origins of Paper Money
academic.text:
Paper money first appeared in China more than a thousand years ago. Merchants during the Tang dynasty found heavy metal coins inconvenient for large transactions, so they began leaving their coins with trusted agents in exchange for paper receipts. These receipts could be traded among merchants and later exchanged back for coins.
By the eleventh century, the Song government had recognized the usefulness of this system and began issuing official paper notes. Government control brought both advantages and risks. On the one hand, official notes were accepted throughout the empire. On the other hand, the government could print as many notes as it wished, and during times of war it often printed far more than it could support. The result was inflation: prices rose sharply, and the notes lost much of their value.
European travelers such as Marco Polo described Chinese paper money with amazement, but the idea spread slowly. It was not until the seventeenth century that banks in Sweden and England began issuing paper notes of their own. Today, paper money is used everywhere, although electronic payments are steadily replacing it in many countries.

questions.q: Why did merchants in the Tang dynasty begin using paper receipts?
options: Metal coins were inconvenient for large payments.
Paper was cheaper to produce than metal.
Foreign traders refused to accept coins.
questions.why: „found heavy metal coins inconvenient for large transactions“.

questions.q: The word "issuing" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: issue = (offiziell) ausgeben.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what was a disadvantage of government-controlled paper money?
options: It was accepted only in a few cities.
Criminals found it far too easy to make copies of the official notes.
The government sometimes printed too much, which caused prices to rise.
Merchants could not exchange it for coins.
questions.why: Zu viel gedrucktes Geld → Inflation.

questions.q: Why does the author mention Marco Polo?
options: To describe a famous Chinese merchant
To argue that paper money was invented in Europe
To explain how paper money quickly reached Europe through trade
To show that Europeans found Chinese paper money remarkable
questions.why: Er beschrieb das Papiergeld „with amazement“.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last sentence of the passage?
options: Paper money may become less common in the future.

Paper money is no longer printed.
Electronic payments are less secure than cash.
questions.why: Elektronische Zahlungen ersetzen Papiergeld „steadily“.

academic.title: The Science of Habits
academic.text:
Psychologists define a habit as a behavior that has become automatic through repetition. According to one widely used model, every habit consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. The cue is a trigger, such as a time of day or a feeling. The routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is the benefit the brain receives, which makes it more likely that the behavior will be repeated.
Research suggests that habits form gradually. In one study, participants who tried to adopt a new daily behavior, such as eating fruit at lunch, needed an average of about two months before the action felt automatic. The time varied widely, however, from less than three weeks to almost a year, depending on the person and the complexity of the behavior.
Because cues are so powerful, experts often recommend changing the environment rather than relying on willpower alone. Someone who wants to snack less, for example, might simply avoid keeping chips at home. Likewise, placing running shoes next to the door can serve as a cue that makes exercise easier to start.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what is the role of the reward?
options: It replaces the cue that started the behavior.
It makes the behavior more likely to be repeated.
It reduces the need for repetition.
It signals the start of a routine.
questions.why: Die Belohnung macht Wiederholung wahrscheinlicher.

questions.q: The word "gradually" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: gradually = allmählich.

questions.q: What did the study described in paragraph 2 find?
options: Complex habits form faster than simple ones in most people.
Eating fruit is the easiest habit to form.
All habits form in exactly two months.
The time needed to form a habit differed greatly between people.
questions.why: Von unter drei Wochen bis fast ein Jahr.

questions.q: Why does the author mention running shoes?
options: To give an example of using the environment as a cue
To recommend a particular type of shoe
To show that exercise is an especially difficult habit to form
questions.why: Schuhe an der Tür als Auslöser.

questions.q: What can be inferred about willpower?
options: It may be less effective than changing one's surroundings.
It has no connection to habits.
It is the most important factor in forming habits.
questions.why: „changing the environment rather than relying on willpower alone“.

academic.title: The Journey of Coffee
academic.text:
Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world, and it has a surprisingly long history. According to a well-known story, a goat herder in Ethiopia noticed that his goats became very energetic after eating red berries from a certain bush. He tried the berries himself and felt more awake.
Whether or not the story is true, we know that by the fifteenth century, people in Yemen were roasting coffee beans and making a drink from them. Coffee houses soon opened in cities across the Middle East. They became popular places where people met to talk, listen to music, and share news.
In the seventeenth century, coffee arrived in Europe. At first, some people were suspicious of the new drink, but it quickly became fashionable. Today, coffee is grown in more than fifty countries, and Brazil produces more coffee than any other nation.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
questions.why: Der Text erzählt die Geschichte des Kaffees.

questions.q: According to the story, what did the goat herder notice?
options: The bush grew much faster than other plants nearby.
His goats had more energy after eating certain berries.
questions.why: „became very energetic after eating red berries“.

questions.q: What does the author say about the goat herder story?
options: It is only told in Europe.
questions.why: „Whether or not the story is true …“

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what did people do in coffee houses?
questions.why: „met to talk, listen to music, and share news“.

questions.q: Which country produces the most coffee today?
questions.why: „Brazil produces more coffee than any other nation“.

academic.title: The Problem of Antibiotic Resistance
academic.text:
Since their introduction in the 1940s, antibiotics have transformed medicine, turning once-fatal infections into routine illnesses. Yet their very success has created a formidable problem. Bacteria reproduce rapidly, and random genetic mutations occasionally render some individuals less vulnerable to a particular drug. When an antibiotic is administered, susceptible bacteria die, but resistant ones survive and multiply, gradually producing populations that the drug can no longer control.
Compounding this process, bacteria can exchange genetic material directly, sometimes even across species, through a mechanism known as horizontal gene transfer. A resistance gene that arises in one organism may therefore spread far more quickly than inheritance alone would allow.
Human behavior accelerates the problem. Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for viral infections, against which they are entirely ineffective, and patients often stop treatment once symptoms subside, potentially leaving the hardiest bacteria alive. Meanwhile, pharmaceutical companies have little financial incentive to develop new antibiotics, which are typically used sparingly and for short periods, making them far less profitable than medications for chronic conditions.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why do resistant bacteria become more common?
options: They reproduce more slowly than other bacteria.
They survive treatment while other bacteria die.
questions.why: Empfindliche sterben, resistente vermehren sich.

questions.q: The word "formidable" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.why: formidable = gewaltig, schwerwiegend.

questions.q: What does paragraph 2 suggest about horizontal gene transfer?
options: It makes bacteria more vulnerable to drugs.
It lets resistance spread faster than through reproduction alone.
It only occurs within a single species.
It prevents new mutations from appearing in most types of bacteria.
questions.why: „far more quickly than inheritance alone would allow“.

questions.q: Why does the author mention viral infections?
options: To compare the size of viruses with the size of bacteria
To show that antibiotics work against viruses
To give an example of antibiotics being used inappropriately
To explain how viruses become resistant
questions.why: Antibiotika wirken nicht gegen Viren, werden aber verschrieben.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why few new antibiotics are developed?
options: Scientists believe enough antibiotics already exist.
They are illegal in many countries.
They cannot be tested on patients.
They are not very profitable for drug companies.
questions.why: „little financial incentive … far less profitable“.
